title: "06 · Regression for fair comparison"
subtitle: "Estimate relationships while making adjustment assumptions explicit."

::: {.topic-banner}
**The clinical question**

Does the group difference persist after accounting for credible alternative explanations?
:::

::: {.learning-outcomes}
### By the end of this topic

- Explain regression as a tool for estimation and adjustment.
- Distinguish linear regression for continuous outcomes from logistic regression for binary outcomes.
- Interpret coefficients and odds ratios in clinical language.
- Explain “holding other variables constant” and why it does not automatically remove bias.
:::

## Core ideas

Linear regression estimates an average change in a continuous outcome associated with a one-unit change in a predictor. Logistic regression models a binary outcome and commonly reports odds ratios. Adjustment compares patients who have the same values of included covariates—but only for the structure the model represents.

::: {.clinical-lens}
**Ask:** Why was each variable included? Is it a confounder, mediator, collider, or merely available? A longer model is not necessarily a fairer model.
:::

## R checkpoint

```r
#| eval: false

linear_model <- lm(outcome ~ treatment + age + baseline_score, data = analysis_data)
logistic_model <- glm(event ~ treatment + age, data = analysis_data, family = binomial())
```
